Treatment of SPS has resulted in varying degrees
of ef ���cacy, including remission of symptoms, and is
centered around the use of GABA-ergic agonists.
Diazepam and other benzodiazepines titrated to the
extent of the patient’ s symptoms are utilized as long-
term maintenance therapy. Antispasmodic agents,
such as baclofen and tizanidine, are also helpful for
symptomatic control. 18 Limiting triggers of spells by
mitigating external stimuli —in one case sounds and
visual stimulation in an intensive care unit —also
allows for tighter control of spell provocation and
frequency.4 Immunomodulation with steroids, IV
immunoglobulin, and plasmapheresis is also utilized,
particularly during acute exacerbations of symp-
toms and hospitalizations. 7,10,18

Discussion
Although the cause of SPS is still unknown, a theory
based on the hindrance of gamma-aminobutyric acid
(GABA) production has been proposed in the liter-
ature. Patients with SPS often present with elevated
levels of intrathecal autoantibodies to glutamic acid
decarboxylase (the GAD65 subtype), the rate-limiting
enzyme for GABA synthesis. The decreased produc-
tion of the inhibitory neurotransmitter has been
implicated in the constellation of centrally-mediated
muscle group activation present in SPS.
5,9 Remark-
ably, a decrease in central GABA transmission has
also been associated with anxiety disorders, sleep
disorders, depression, and posttraumatic stress
disorder.
11 A case report described the diagnosis of
SPS after a precipitating event leading to posttrau-
matic stress disorder suggesting a common physiologic
causal pathway between the two.
12 SPS has also been
associated with numerous autoimmune conditions,
including hypothyroidism and diabetes 4,5—with our
patient presenting with subclinical hypothyroidism,
with antithyroid peroxidase antibodies, as well as islet
cell antibodies that may predispose to the development
of diabetes later in life.
